description: Kartik is the CTO of a technology platform, with experience building both conventional software and AI solutions in production. On Field Aide, Kartik led the product, the engine and the deployment. Amrita works in the aerospace sector, on embedded systems. On Field Aide, Amrita shaped the voice-first design for farmers who cannot read, and the look of the app.
summary: Field Aide is a voice and picture assistant, in Hindi and English, for rainfed farmers in Vidarbha, Maharashtra (Akola, Buldhana and Washim). Many of these farmers leave their fields bare for months after soybean, and many cannot read. With one tap, Field Aide talks to the farmer like a phone call, asking a few questions about their farm, water and priorities. Each answer can be spoken or tapped on a picture. It then compares four ways to use the field through the year: their current rotation, soybean then chickpea, cotton with pigeon pea, and soybean then winter sorghum. Results are spoken and drawn as a twelve-month bar showing when the field is covered and when it is bare. Hot months and dry spells come from 45 years of NASA POWER weather, and crop seasons are seen in MODIS satellite greenness. Each choice comes with what is checked, what is only estimated, and what to ask a local expert. This matters because bare soil loses water and topsoil, and changing weather makes old crop calendars less reliable. Field Aide supports, and does not replace, the judgement of farmers and local experts.
details:
Field Aide - A voice and picture assistant in Hindi and English that helps rainfed farmers in Vidarbha, Maharashtra, plan how to use their field through the whole year, built on NASA Earth data.

Live app: https://field-shift-opal.vercel.app

Code: https://github.com/kmcodes/space-apps

What it does and how it works -

Many rainfed farmers in Akola, Buldhana and Washim grow soybean in the monsoon and then leave the field bare for months. Bare soil loses moisture and topsoil, and changing weather makes old crop calendars less reliable.

Field Aide works like a phone call:

i. One tap starts the conversation. The app greets the farmer and asks a few short questions aloud: where the farm is, what they grow now, where their water comes from, what matters most to them, how much water they have, whether they own a sprayer or sowing machine, and where they sell. Each answer can be spoken or tapped on a picture, and every option is read aloud while its picture lights up. A form offers the same questions to people who prefer to read.

ii. The phone’s location is confirmed on a satellite map with a pin. Farms outside our three districts are told so early and can still see an example.(This feature is avaialble only if the user is present in Vidarbha region of Maharastra else the user has to use the fallback options available in the app.)

iii. An engine compares four ways to use the field through the year: the farmer’s current rotation, soybean then chickpea, cotton with pigeon pea, and soybean then winter sorghum.

iv. The results are spoken and drawn as pictures, with no scores on screen. The best choices get a 'thumbs-up'. Each choice has a twelve-month bar grouped into kharif, rabi and summer, with one colour per crop and black for a bare field. The hot months and long dry spells from 45 years of weather are marked under it. Three rows speak when tapped: checked advice, estimated advice and what to ask a local expert. Sources sit behind a “for experts” link.

Under the hood. For every year from 1981 to 2025, the engine scores each rotation on:

a) water fit

b) sowing and harvest timing

c) days the field stays bare

d) nitrogen from legumes

e) fodder value

f) a price signal from mandi prices

The farmer’s first priority gets a fixed 40% of the weight and a second priority 20%, and the weights are shown. Scoring all 45 years gives a range instead of one number, and close results are reported as a tie. A rotation scored on less than 70% of the information that matters is not ranked, so a gap can never make a choice look better.

Benefits

a) The app reaches farmers who cannot read, through voice, pictures and a twelve-month picture of the field.

b) Shows the bare-field months that cost soil moisture and topsoil, next to rotations that keep the field covered.

c) Matches the farmer’s own goal: saving water, fodder for animals, less fertiliser, less soil washing away, healthier soil or a better price.

d) Marks the risky months (heat, and dry spells inside the monsoon), so a farmer sees when a crop would be exposed.

e) Is honest about what it does not know. Every suggestion is labelled an estimate until its inputs are checked, and it tells the farmer what to confirm with a Krishi Vigyan Kendra officer or agronomist.

f) Works on an ordinary phone in the browser, installs to the home screen, and costs the farmer nothing.

Intended impact

Field Aide turns decades of NASA observations into a conversation a farmer can have in their own language, so that the empty months after soybean become a decision, not a habit. It aims to start better conversations between farmers and local experts, not to replace them: every suggestion is a hypothesis for local review. The engine and the language layer are built so that Marathi, more districts and more crops can be added without a rewrite, once native speakers and agronomists have reviewed the content.

Field Aide supports, and does not replace, the judgement of farmers and local agricultural experts. This line is visible on every screen, in Hindi and English.

Data source for Field Aide

NASA POWER (daily, 1981–2025) -> Rain, temperature, soil wetness, humidity and sunlight: monsoon onset and withdrawal, dry spells, heat days, water fit

NASA MODIS MOD13Q1 NDVI (250 m, 2015–2025, via AppEEARS) -> Crop seasons and bare-field windows seen from space

ERA5 reanalysis (via Open-Meteo) -> Independent cross-check of POWER. Both agree rain has risen but disagree on heat days, so we show a range and claim no heat trend

ISRIC SoilGrids -> Clay, sand, pH and soil carbon

Agmarknet mandi prices (data.gov.in) and minimum support prices -> Three years of district prices for the price signal

FAO-56, FAO Training Manual 3, ICAR-CRIDA Akola plan, ICRISAT, PDKV Akola, FAO ECOCROP -> Crop water needs, sowing windows, durations and heat thresholds, each marked valid or unverified

Tools, languages and software

Data pipeline : Python, pandas, NumPy, SciPy; NASA earthaccess; AppEEARS

Engine and API : Python rules engine with 170 automated tests (pytest); FastAPI; hosted on Render

App : Next.js, React and TypeScript, Tailwind CSS; installable web app (PWA); hosted on Vercel

Voice : The browser’s built-in speech recognition and speech synthesis, in Hindi and English (Sarvam AI speech planned)

Testing and media : Playwright with Microsoft Edge, for screenshots and the demo recording

Hardware : No special hardware: an ordinary Android phone with Chrome

Collaboration : Git and GitHub; Claude Code (Anthropic) as a coding assistant, directed and reviewed by the team

How it is creative

i) A phone call, not a dashboard. Built for low literacy: one tap, then a spoken conversation with picture answers.

ii) The year as a picture. A twelve-month bar shows when the field is covered and when it is bare, so the whole plan is visible without reading.

iii) Honesty built into the engine. A missing input is never scored as zero, every evidence line names its dataset, period and validity, and where two datasets disagree we show both.

iv) No invented words or numbers. No language model writes anything the farmer sees: every sentence is a template filled from engine fields.

v) Two languages from one engine. Hindi and English today, with Marathi designed in.

[Insert image] For experts, every source:

Factors we considered

i) Literacy: voice first, pictures second, text last.

ii) Language: Hindi for the demo. Marathi, the region’s language, waits for a native reviewer, and all Hindi text needs a native speaker’s check.

iii) Scale of the data: weather is on a 25–50 km grid and satellite pixels are 250 m, so the app never claims field-level precision.

iv) Trust: scores rank ideas; they don’t predict yield or profit. The expert link and the “ask a local expert” row keep people in the loop.

v) Privacy: nothing about the farmer is stored, and coordinates are rounded before any outside service sees them.

vi) Phones and networks: the free server is woken as soon as the app opens and retried automatically, and the app works by touch when voice isn’t available.

vii) Accessibility: large buttons, moving sound waves on the speak button, and motion that stops when the phone asks for less.

What is not done yet

i) Every suggestion is still an estimate, because most crop inputs are unverified.

ii) Speech uses the browser’s voices; Sarvam AI speech is planned.

iii) Hindi text is machine-drafted and not yet reviewed by a native speaker; Marathi is not built.

iv) Sunn hemp and horse gram are scored but not shown, because their data is too thin.
